analysis.one_liner: Bars EPA power-plant carbon rules unless U.S.-only benefits are counted, and voids two proposed rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee after its July 30, 2014 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the EPA from issuing or enforcing any rule limiting carbon dioxide from power plants unless the agency's cost-benefit analysis primarily counted only benefits inside the United States and reported them separately from global benefits [S2][S3]. It would also erase, as if never issued, the EPA's two proposed power plant carbon rules from 2014 — one for new power plants and one for existing ones [S2][S3]. Because climate benefits are inherently global while pollution-control costs fall on U.S. utilities and ratepayers, this requirement would make such rules nearly impossible to justify on paper [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal-fired power plants and the coal mining industry, which would avoid the cost of complying with the proposed carbon rules, and electric utilities generally facing fewer federal emission limits. Some ratepayers might see smaller near-term electricity rate increases, the concern supporters of the bill raised.

how_it_helps.text: Would void the EPA's proposed rules for new and existing power plant carbon emissions, so those rules would 'have no force or effect' as if never issued [S2][S3].

Would require the EPA to primarily consider domestic (U.S.-only) benefits, rather than global benefits, in any analysis of power plant carbon rules, and to base its cost-benefit comparison on domestic figures alone [S3].
Would apply to any current or future rule addressing carbon dioxide from electric utility generating units, not just the two named rules [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People exposed to power plant pollution, since the EPA's proposed limits on carbon dioxide from both new and existing power plants would be erased [S2][S3]. Down the line, the costs of unchecked climate change — more severe heat waves, storms, and other damage — would fall broadly on the public, while cheaper public-health gains from reduced pollution worldwide would no longer be counted in the EPA's decision-making.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public breathing power plant pollution

drawbacks.text: The bill would erase two proposed EPA rules limiting carbon emissions from power plants, removing protections against pollution linked to climate change and air-quality harms [S2][S3].

Requiring the EPA to weigh only domestic benefits would ignore most of the benefits of curbing carbon emissions, since climate change is a global problem; the strongest version of the supporters' argument is that American ratepayers should not pay compliance costs justified mainly by benefits accruing abroad, and an honest assessment is that this accounting change, combined with the nullification, would make it very hard for the EPA to protect against power plant carbon pollution at all [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real effect would be to nullify the EPA's 2014 proposed power plant carbon rules and make future ones almost impossible to justify [S2][S3]. Supporters could fairly point to electricity rate concerns for coal-dependent regions like Missouri and West Virginia, whose representatives introduced the bill [S3]. But the cost side — weaker pollution protections and an accounting rule designed to defeat the rules — outweighs the near-term rate savings, and the bill's backers offered no replacement policy for limiting power plant carbon emissions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Ann Wagner introduced the bill on July 30, 2014, joined by 10 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on August 1, 2014 to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's existing protections stayed intact: the EPA's proposed power plant carbon rules were not erased and remained on track to be finalized, while coal operators and coal-fired utilities did not get the compliance relief the bill would have given them. The outcome also spared the EPA from the domestic-benefits-only accounting requirement.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 30, 2014, sent it to the Energy and Power Subcommittee on August 1, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, and the bill died in a committee without action [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired electric generation
industries.note: The bill would void the EPA's proposed carbon rules for existing and new power plants and bar future ones unless U.S.-only benefits were counted [S2][S3]. Its gain — avoiding emission limits — comes at the public's cost of continued power plant carbon pollution.

Utilities would avoid compliance costs under the proposed rules, but the bill's nullification of existing-source standards would also remove the regulatory certainty some utilities sought for long-term investment planning [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Natural gas and renewable energy producers
industries.note: The proposed rules were expected to shift generation away from coal toward gas and renewables; voiding them removes that market push, so the industry's loss runs alongside the public's loss of emission reductions [S2].
